chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Hasan, from Ali ibn Asbat, from Tha'labah, from Abu al-Hasan Umar ibn Shaddad al-Azdi, and al-Sarri, both from Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
"A man has the most right to his wealth as long as the soul is in him; if he bequeaths all of it, it is valid for him."

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The implication of this report, from his saying 'if he bequeaths all of it, it is valid for him,' is a conjecture of the narrator, because the bequest is not executed except in the third, as we will clarify later, unless with the consent and approval of the heirs. Rather, he has the most right to his wealth by spending it during his life on what he prefers and chooses. It is also possible that the meaning of the report is that if he has no heir, near or distant, then it is permissible for him at that time to bequeath all his wealth however he wishes. And that which indicates this is what he narrated:

key_terms.إِنْ أَوْصَى بِهِ كُلَّهُ: If he bequeaths all of it
key_terms.الرَّجُلُ أَحَقُّ بِمَالِهِ: The man has the most right to his wealth

ai.seo_question: Can a person bequeath all their wealth in a will according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration to discuss the scope of a man's authority over his wealth, where the initial report suggests unrestricted bequest. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan provides critical scholarly analysis, distinguishing between the right to spend during life and the legal limit of one-third for bequests to non-heirs, attributing the 'all wealth' claim to a narrator's error or a specific case of heirlessness. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that full disposal requires either the absence of heirs or their explicit consent.
